key_insight: Fewer than 2% of FDA-authorized AI medical devices are prognostic, and those that are vary widely in prediction horizon (minutes to years), highlighting a regulatory and ethical gap as prognostic tools become more common.
problem_solved: Identifies and quantifies the underrepresentation of prognostic AI devices among FDA-authorized tools and highlights the need to address associated regulatory and ethical challenges before their numbers grow.
method: Systematic analysis of FDA-authorized AI/ML medical devices to classify devices as prognostic versus non-prognostic
Characterization of prognostic tools by prediction horizon (short to long-term) and assessment of regulatory and ethical implications
Synthesis of findings to recommend areas requiring regulatory attention and ethical guidance
impact: Raises awareness for AI/ML practitioners and regulators that prognostic models are rare but diverse in scope, signaling the need for clearer approval pathways, validation standards, and ethical safeguards tailored to time-horizon and clinical impact.
visual_elements: Pie chart showing proportion of FDA-authorized devices that are prognostic (<2%) versus other types
Bar or violin plot displaying distribution of prediction horizons (minutes, hours, days, months, years)
Flowchart mapping regulatory and ethical challenges across stages: development → validation → deployment → monitoring
Icon-based checklist of recommended safeguards (transparency, calibration, post-market surveillance, informed consent)
paper_title: Authorization of prognostic AI medical devices
paper_authors: Urs J. Muehlematter, Kerstin Noelle Vokinger
